Every contract requires consideration (something of value that is exchanged or promised on both sides). Copyright is a contract between the general public and producers of works. The contract is basically: You produce something, we will grant you a temporary monopoly over that work in exchange for the work being put into the public domain.

Because the copyright term has been extended every time when works are supposed to enter the public domain, the public's end of the deal has not been fulfilled, and might never be fulfilled as politicians who vote to extend the term seem to no shame in supporting obscene term lengths. The enforcement of a temporary monopoly has public costs (direct and indirect), and the public's side of the contract has never been fulfilled with works entering the public domain in recent history. As long as this remains the case, then the court should not consider copyright to be legally binding on the basis of one-sided & unfair consideration. If and when works do enter the public domain, they are of so little value, that the public will not receive fair consideration. This is something to consider if you ever serve as a juror in a trial that deals with copyright. Legal information is not legal advice. This is not legal advice.
